title: I don't eat pork
title_target: ဝက်သား မစားဘူး — wèk-tha: ma.sa:-boo:
goal: Order food, describe flavors, and explain what you don't eat clearly and politely — something many travelers need, for reasons of faith, health, or taste, and that Burmese textbooks rarely cover.

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — Mohinga for breakfast
dialogs.intro: Mya Mya takes Ani out for mohinga, Myanmar's national dish. Notice how Ani explains what she can't eat: she says what she **doesn't** eat first, then immediately offers an alternative — a way that keeps the host from feeling awkward.

lines.speaker: မြမြ:
lines.text: [အာနီ|a-nee]၊ [မုန့်ဟင်းခါး|mohⁿ.-hiⁿ:-hka:] [စား|sa:] [ဖူး|hpoo:] [လား|la:]။
lines.id: Ani, have you ever had mohinga?

lines.speaker: အာနီ:
lines.text: [မစားဖူးသေးဘူး|ma.sa:-hpoo:-thay:-boo:]။ [ဘာ|ba] [နဲ့|nè.] [လုပ်|lohk] [လဲ|lè:]။
lines.id: Not yet. What's it made with?

lines.speaker: မြမြ:
lines.text: [ငါး|nga:] [နဲ့|nè.] [ခေါက်ဆွဲ|hkowk-hswè:] [ပါ|ba]။ [ငါးပိ|nga.pee.] [လည်း|lè:] [ပါ|pa] [တယ်|dè]။
lines.id: Fish and noodles. There's fish paste in it too.

lines.text: [ဝက်သား|wèk-tha:] [ပါ|pa] [လား|la:]။ [ကျွန်မ|cha.ma.] [ဝက်သား|wèk-tha:] [မစားဘူး|ma.sa:-boo:]။

lines.literal: pig-meat — included — Q? I(f) — pig-meat — not-eat.

lines.text: [မပါဘူး|ma.pa-boo:]။ [ငါး|nga:] [ပဲ|bè:] [ပါ|pa] [တယ်|dè]။ [စိတ်ချ|sayk-hcha.] [ပါ|ba]။

grammars.title: ⚠️ Explaining what you don't eat, politely
body: Myanmar is a mostly Buddhist country, and pork appears in many of its dishes. Stating a dietary restriction isn't unusual there — what matters is **how** you say it, because a Burmese host easily feels they've failed their guest.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ကျွန်မ မွတ်စလင်ပါ
ဝက်သား မစားဘူး
အသား မစားဘူး
ကြက်သားနဲ့ ငါး ရပါတယ်
ဝက်သား ပါလား
အရက် မသောက်ဘူး

after: The key is the order: **say what you can't have, then right away say what you can.** "I don't eat pork, but chicken and fish are fine" saves the whole conversation, while stopping after the first half leaves your host wondering what on earth to serve.

⚠️ Notice ပါလား (*pa-la:*) — "is it included?". The ပါ here isn't the politeness particle but a verb meaning "be included, come with", and it's the word you use to ask what's in a dish. ငါးပိ ပါလား = "is there fish paste in it?"

grammars.title: Flavors are VERBS
body: Burmese has no true adjectives. "Spicy" isn't an adjective but a verb meaning "to be spicy", so it takes the ending တယ် directly and is negated with မ … ဘူး, just like any other verb. Unit 14 covers this fully; for today, just get a feel for the pattern.
after: ⚠️ "Delicious" has no single word: Burmese uses စားလို့ကောင်းတယ်, literally "good for eating". For drinks, use သောက်လို့ကောင်းတယ်. Praising your host's cooking with this sentence never fails.

grammars.title: မ … ပါနဲ့ — a gentle "don't"
body: Prohibitions are formed with မ before the verb and နဲ့ after it. Slipping ပါ in between turns an order into a request.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: ထည့်မပေးပါနဲ့
အရမ်း မချိုပါနဲ့

after: ⚠️ Don't confuse it with the နဲ့ meaning "with" (unit 3). The position makes it clear: နဲ့ meaning "with" attaches to a **noun**; နဲ့ meaning "don't" attaches to a **verb** that already starts with မ.

grammars.title: …ဖူး — ever
body: ဖူး (*hpoo:*) is inserted before the sentence ending and means "have ever", in the sense of life experience. It's your first doorway into talking about the past, covered fully in unit 17.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: မစားဖူးဘူး
have you ever been to Myanmar?

after: Tell **မဖူးဘူး** (never, and no plans to) apart from **မဖူးသေးဘူး** (not yet, but maybe someday). Adding သေး makes your answer sound open and friendly — very useful when you're offered something you don't know.

blocks.text: This list is enough to read almost any food-stall menu and order without pointing. Notice that meat words are formed by attaching သား (*tha:*, "meat") to the animal's name — so one word unlocks four.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: မုန့်ဟင်းခါး
လက်ဖက်သုပ်
ဟင်းသီးဟင်းရွက်

blocks.title: Three things about the Burmese table
items: **မုန့်ဟင်းခါး is the national breakfast**, sold from roadside carts from dawn and gone by midday. The broth is made from fish and banana stem, without pork — so it's usually safe for those who avoid pork, but still worth asking about, because every stall is different.

**လက်ဖက်သုပ်** (*la.hpèk-thohk*) is a salad of fermented tea leaves mixed with fried beans, garlic, and tomato. Myanmar is one of the few countries in the world that **eats** tea leaves rather than just brewing them. Try it once; it tastes like nothing you've ever eaten.

⚠️ **ငါးပိ** (*nga.pee.*) — fermented fish paste — is in almost every Burmese dish, much like fish sauce in Thai cooking. It smells strong, tastes savory, and isn't meat. If you don't like it, say ငါးပိ မထည့်ပါနဲ့.
